The vote passed 137-7, though opposition Fidesz and KDNP lawmakers boycotted the session. The NVVH, a flagship institution of the Tisza government, is tasked with recovering misused public assets and identifying officials who enabled corruption. Unger’s mandate begins on Sept. 1. She cautioned that while indictments may be issued, final legal judgments in corruption cases will take time, prompting debate over the pace of the anti-corruption drive. by Euractiv | Aug. 29, 2026, 5:08 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Hungarian political scientist Anna Unger (L) takes her oath with her deputy Katalin Tasnadi (R) after being elected by the National Assembly in a secret ballot on Aug. 28, 2026, for the head and deputy chief of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH). (Photo by Attila KISBENEDEK / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Hungary’s parliament elected political analyst Anna Unger on Friday to head the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), a flagship institution of the Tisza government’s anti-corruption drive. The NVVH, created in July, is an independent body tasked with tracing and recovering misused public assets and identifying officials who enabled abuses. It reports to parliament and can access financial and official records, investigate cases and refer them for prosecution. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . The motion passed with 137 votes in favour and seven against. Most MPs from the opposition Fidesz and KDNP walked out before the vote, continuing their boycott of an institution they have branded a “new ÁVH” – a reference to Hungary’s communist-era secret police. Advertisement Despite Tisza’s supermajority, the selection process exposed some internal dissent . One Tisza MP, Márton Melléthei-Barna, confirmed he voted against Unger, saying he preferred fellow candidate Miklós Ligeti on professional grounds. The PhD controversy Unger, a prominent democracy researcher at ELTE University, is no stranger to political controversy, though recent criticism has also come from liberal circles. In late 2024, Unger faced a backlash over her role as an official reviewer of the doctoral dissertation of Balázs Orbán, then political director to former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Critics questioned why the university was facilitating a PhD for a senior official from a government that had repeatedly clashed with academic institutions. Unger defended her role, arguing that educators should not discriminate between students on the basis of political affiliation. She later said the controversy had made her “bulletproof” against public attacks. Identifying ‘facilitators’ During her parliamentary hearing, Unger said the office should focus not only on recovering assets but also on identifying the institutional chains and decision-makers that enabled corruption. Advertisement “Who were the players who assisted in this? Who was the prosecutor who did not initiate proceedings? Who in the central bank failed to prevent the loss of assets but did nothing against it?” Unger asked. She said officials tasked with protecting the public purse but who failed to act should be identified. Unger also warned against expecting immediate results, noting that while six years could be enough to bring indictments, final judgments often take much longer in Hungary’s legal system. Her comments prompted accusations of “sabotage” from former prime ministerial candidate Péter Márki-Zay. Magyar defended the appointment, saying that while criminal proceedings take time, his government remained committed to changing the status quo. Unger’s mandate will begin on 1 September. The office is still seeking three additional deputies after previous applications were declared invalid. See the original by Mátyás Varga here . Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters Kamala Harris Kamala Harris’s California home targeted by trespasser, officials say Former vice-president and her husband were not home when person entered their property, no arrests were made Jessica Glenza Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.08 EDT First published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 10.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Law enforcement officials and a spokesperson for former vice-president Kamala Harris said a trespasser was stopped at her Malibu home in California on Friday night. Neither the former vice-president nor her husband, Doug Emhoff, were home at the time. “Security personnel stopped an individual who illegally entered Vice-President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff’s property before the individual reached the home,” Harris spokesperson Eduardo Negrón said in a statement on Saturday, reported by Politico . “Vice-President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff were not present. They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly.” Malibu Lost Hills sheriff’s deputies responded to Harris’s home around 10.30pm that Friday night on a report of a “suspicious person”, according to a statement from the Los Angeles county sheriff’s department, after private security had stopped the individual. “The individual who was outside of the property upon our arrival was warned and advised by deputies to leave the premises and left voluntarily without incident,” the sheriff’s department said in a statement. “A trespassing report was taken. Sheriff’s Malibu Lost Hills Deputies will increase patrols in the area as a precaution.” The incident was originally reported by TMZ . Vice-presidents in the US typically receive six months of Secret Service protection after leaving office. Former president Joe Biden extended Harris’s security detail to 18 months before leaving office. That extension was canceled in August 2025 by Donald Trump. Ex-presidents typically receive security protection for life. Harris bought the home in the Point Dume area of Malibu for $8.1m this May , which prompted speculation that she would not run for president again. The celebrity studded retreat is typically seen as a place where people “ downshift ”, according to a Politico article at the time. Image: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP KYIV, Ukraine — A Russian-guided bomb exploded next to public buses filled with passengers in eastern Ukraine, authorities said Thursday, killing 30 people as part of a wave of attacks that also worsened power outages in the capital. The morning attack occurred next to a bus stop in the war-torn city of Kramatorsk in Ukraine's Donetsk region, prompting public transport to be suspended in the area. "There is no doubt that Russia is cynically targeting civilians," Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the city's military administration, said, adding that the rescue effort had been hampered by subsequent Russian attacks using small drones. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Russia has escalated its aerial attack in recent weeks, putting pressure on Ukraine as it prepares for winter and hitting the infrastructure keeping its war-battered economy afloat. Recent targets have included energy systems, key industries, railways, post offices, shopping centers, telecom networks, gas stations and grain exports. A rescue worker sits on the ground next to a residential building destroyed in a Russian missile strike on Pryluky, Ukraine, Wednesday. Image: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Thursday's attack followed a Russian missile strike a day earlier that killed 22, including five children, in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky. Rescuers were searching the rubble of a residential building. At least 54 people were wounded. Several survivors slept in heavily damaged apartments because they couldn't find anywhere else to stay. Ukraine appeals for more defense support from NATO Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy traveled to Pryluky on Thursday with visiting British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who announced new sanctions on Russia. Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries. "It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine's defense," he wrote in an online post. "Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day." In audio clips responding to journalist's questions Thursday evening, Zelenskyy said a Ukrainian delegation would meet in the U.S. with President Donald Trump's representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff for two days beginning Friday to discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses, among other issues. Ukraine's energy company DTEK said national grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power outages in Kyiv. Regular, rolling outages that occur on a schedule across the country will be halted during these shutdowns. Officials are urging families to prepare emergency kits, store drinking water and maintain backup power sources, as Moscow keeps up the intensity of its attacks. Kyiv police said bomb disposal specialists defused two unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings. Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv's Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said. Ukrainian attacks damage data center and oil refinery Russian technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline. Also Thursday, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified. Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said most of the drones were shot down by air defenses, but one "reached a northern industrial hub." He didn't elaborate. Russian independent news outlet Astra reported that the Omsk oil refinery was on fire after the attack. There was no official confirmation of the report. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his government presented proposals to both Russia and Ukraine aimed at protecting civilian shipping in the Black Sea, while warning that commercial trade and grain exports could be disrupted by escalating military offensives. Separately, Lithuania deployed about 100 additional soldiers to help secure the NATO member's border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, the Baltic country's defense minister, Robertas Kaunas, said. Sandwiched between Lithuania and Poland, Kaliningrad is separated from mainland Russia and remains a major security concern for NATO's eastern flank. © 2026 NPR More from NPR
